title: the Purusha Sukta
hook: the hymn's eleventh verse is a string of questions: when they divided the Purusha, what was his mouth? the answer has been argued over hard

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Purusha Sukta's great offering: spring as butter, summer as fuel, autumn as the offering, and from it creatures, chants and verses. What grew out of something you gave? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-nine.

When they divided the Purusha, into how many parts did they arrange him? What was his mouth? What were his arms? What are his thighs and feet called? That's the Purusha Sukta's eleventh verse, in paraphrase, and it's nothing but questions, like a teacher quizzing a class before the answer comes. The answer comes in the next verse. It's short. And it has been recited, defended and fought over. Today: the verse about the body's parts, and the honest argument around it.
screen: `WHAT WAS HIS MOUTH? HIS ARMS?` → `A VERSE OF QUESTIONS.` → `AN ANSWER THAT'S BEEN FOUGHT OVER.`

segments.voice: Verse twelve answers, in paraphrase: the brahmin, the priest, was his mouth. His arms were made the rajanya, the ruler and warrior. His thighs became the vaishya, the people of trade and farming. From his feet the shudra, the laborer, was born. Four groups, from one body. Notice one thing about the wording. The verse doesn't use the word varna, the later word for these social orders, and it doesn't say higher or lower. It names parts of a single person. But readers have heard a ranking in mouth and feet, and that's where the argument begins. Some traditional readers take the verse as the sacred origin of the four varnas. Over time the verse was also used to defend a ladder fixed by birth, and people outside the four orders altogether were treated as untouchable. Reformers, among them B. R. Ambedkar, attacked that use of the verse directly and fought the system it was used to defend. Other readers, Hindu teachers among them, put the weight elsewhere: all four come from one body, and a body can't live on its mouth alone. Some point to the Bhagavad Gita, where Krishna says the four orders were made according to qualities and actions, and argue that birth was never meant to decide them. These readings don't agree, and this path won't pretend they do. What can be said plainly is what the text says, and what people have done with it. A verse can be held sacred and still need careful hands. That's part of reading any scripture honestly: hearing the words, and also hearing who has been hurt by how they were used.
screen: `MOUTH, ARMS, THIGHS, FEET.` · `ONE BODY. THE WORD VARNA ISN'T THERE.` · `A LADDER BY BIRTH, AND ITS CRITICS.` · `QUALITIES AND ACTIONS, NOT BIRTH?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give every part of the body the same attention. Settle, and breathe. Start at the mouth: notice the lips, the tongue resting. Move to the arms and hands. Then the thighs, their weight on the chair. Then the feet, the part that carries everything and is usually noticed least. Give each the same few breaths, the same care. No part gets more. When you drift, return to wherever you were and continue. If you pray, you can pray for anyone who has been treated as less. The bell holds the time.
The Purusha Sukta. In its twelfth verse, mouth, arms, thighs and feet become four groups of people, and readers have argued over what that means ever since. Today's word.
Your line: the Purusha Sukta. Today, notice someone whose work carries yours and usually goes unthanked, and thank them by name. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Hindus read the Purusha Sukta's verse on the four groups in sharply different ways: some as the origin of the varnas, others as a picture of one interdependent body, and reformers have challenged its use to justify caste by birth.

fork.setup: the hymn asks: when they divided the Purusha, what was his mouth? what does the next verse answer?
fork.reveal: verse twelve: the brahmin was his mouth, the rajanya his arms, the vaishya his thighs, and from his feet the shudra was born. what that means has been argued over hard.

original.note: Sanskrit: the later word for the four social orders; it does not appear in Rig Veda 10.90.12 itself.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Purusha Sukta is the rulebook for caste.
what it means: one verse names four groups as parts of one body, and readers, reformers and teachers have argued over it ever since.
what a scholar hears: brahmano 'sya mukham asid, bahu rajanyah kritah: the verse says rajanya, not kshatriya, and never uses the word varna.
recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home

sources.ref: Rig Veda 10.90.11 (when they divided the Purusha, into how many parts did they arrange him? what was his mouth, his arms, his thighs and feet?)
Rig Veda 10.90.12 (the brahmin was his mouth, the rajanya was made his arms, his thighs the vaishya, from his feet the shudra was born)
Bhagavad Gita 4.13 (the four orders were created by me according to the division of qualities and actions)
B. R. Ambedkar, Who Were the Shudras? (critique of the Purusha Sukta's use to justify caste)

notes: SENSITIVE DAY: the varna verse. The script states the text, then three readings without ranking them: the traditional origin of the varnas; its use to defend caste by birth and untouchability, with Ambedkar's critique; and readings stressing one body and the Gita's qualities-and-actions line. A Keeper, and ideally a Dalit scholar, should check balance and wording.

Historical claims not in the cited text: 'over time the verse was also used to defend a ladder fixed by birth, and people outside the four orders were treated as untouchable'; 'reformers, among them B. R. Ambedkar, attacked that use of the verse directly and fought the system'. Ambedkar's critique is in Who Were the Shudras? Confirm wording.
Text claims to confirm: 10.90.12 reads brāhmaṇo 'sya mukham āsīd bāhū rājanyaḥ kṛtaḥ, ūrū tad asya yad vaiśyaḥ padbhyāṃ śūdro ajāyata; the word varṇa does not appear; rājanya, not kṣatriya, is used.
Glosses: vaishya as 'trade and farming', shudra as 'laborer'; confirm they are fair and not demeaning.

'Some point to the Bhagavad Gita' (4.13, cātur-varṇyaṃ mayā sṛṣṭaṃ guṇa-karma-vibhāgaśaḥ): paraphrased; the Gita uses the word varna there. Confirm the reading 'birth was never meant to decide them' is fairly attributed to some readers, not to the Gita itself.
The hook says the verse has been fought over 'in temples and in politics'; general, confirm or soften.
Editor: cut the speculative 'in ways the poet could hardly have pictured' and the unsourced 'in temples and in politics'; 'holy' framed as 'held sacred' so the narrator does not assert it.
